<|fim_prefix|>Three legal local addresses: IPv4 localhost, IPv6 localhost, IPv4-mapped IPv6 localhost.

## H.4 Path traversal defenses

Multiple layers.

### H.4.1 URL sanity

The request handler rejects (403) any URL that:

- Contains a null byte (`\\0`).
- Contains the literal string `..`.

The check runs BEFORE URL parsing, so encoded variants (`%2e%2e`) are also rejected — URL parsing would normalize them, but the raw-string check catches them first at the pre-parse stage.

### H.4.2 Cart-name regex

Cart names are matched against `/^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$/` per path segment. Legal characters: uppercase letters, lowercase letters, digits, dot, underscore, hyphen. Nothing else.

This excludes:

- Slashes within a segment (safe, since segments are joined with `/`).
- Spaces.
- URL-encoded characters that would decode to interesting characters.
- Null bytes.
<|fim_middle|>- Unicode homoglyphs.
- Control characters.

### H.4.3 Path segment rules

Cart names may contain up to 4 slash-separated segments (`composer/synth-patch/variant-a/version-2`). Each segment:

- Must be 1-128 characters long.
- Must match the regex above.
- Must not be `.` or `..`.

### H.4.4 Resolved-path check

After the cart name is decoded, split, and joined with the cart directory, the resulting path is `path.resolve`'d. The absolute resolved path is compared against the normalized cart directory. If the resolved path does not start with the cart directory prefix (with a trailing separator), the cart is treated as missing (404).

This catches any exotic case the regex misses. Even if a segment slipped through, the resolved path must physically land under the cart directory.

### H.4.5 Existence + file check

The candidate path must exist (`existsSync`) and be a regular file (`statSync().isFile()`). Directories don't serve; missing files 404.

## H.5 Cart-dir resolution

`:cart-dir` is passed to `safeResolveCartDir(cartDir)`. Steps:

<|fim_suffix|>1. Resolve the cart dir against `process.cwd()`.
2. Normalize both the resolved dir and cwd.
3. Fail if the resolved dir does not start with the cwd prefix (or equal cwd).
4. Fail if the resolved dir doesn't exist.
5. Fail if the resolved dir is not a directory.

Failures throw an error at `http/serve` call time. The server does not start with an unsafe cart-dir.

The cwd-escape check means `:cart-dir \"../../etc\"` refuses. So does `:cart-dir \"/absolute/path/outside/cwd\"`.

## H.6 Method restriction

Only GET is accepted. POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, and any other method return 405 with a plain-text body `\"method not allowed\"`.

v1.1 does not accept cart writes over HTTP. Cart edits round-trip through the composer's own `composer/save` and `composer/load`, on the local file system.

## H.7 Content-Type responses

- `text/plain` for the 405 body.
- `text/html; charset=utf-8` for all other successful and error responses.

The server does not serve arbitrary MIME types. It emits HTML shells around cart source. If a later wave adds asset serving (images, audio), it will add explicit MIME-type mapping per file extension.

## H.8 HTML escaping

Every user-controlled string that appears in HTML responses passes through `escapeHtml(s)`:

<|fim_prefix|>(define (eval-expr expr env)
  (cond
    ;; A number evaluates to itself.
    ((number? expr) expr)

    ;; A symbol looks up in the environment.
    ((symbol? expr) (lookup expr env))

    ((pair? expr)
     (case (car expr)
       ((quote) (cadr expr))
<|fim_middle|>       ((if)
        (if (eval-expr (cadr expr) env)

       ((define)
        (extend-env! env (cadr expr) (eval-expr (caddr expr) env)))
       (else
        ;; function call
        (apply-fn (eval-expr (car expr) env)
                  (map (lambda (e) (eval-expr e env))
<|fim_suffix|>                       (cdr expr))))))))

  (list 'closure params body env))

<|fim_prefix|>The metadata is filled in at registration. When you later call `(help 'car)`, the introspection layer reads from this exact object. There is no separate documentation source. The doc lives with the code.

This is what makes the reference manual generatable. `src/docs-emitter.js` walks the registry and produces the manual by concatenating the records. When a verb changes, the manual updates on the next build. There is no drift.

## 2.15 Reading a verb like a datasheet

Here is a workflow for reading a verb record you have never seen before.
<|fim_middle|>
**First pass — the doc.** Read the doc string. That is the one-sentence summary. If the doc string tells you what you need, you can stop.

**Second pass — the arity and contract.** How many arguments does it take? What shape do they have? What does it return? Now you know if it fits your use.

**Third pass — the examples.** Pick the level closest to your current fluency. Read the code. Adapt it to your context.

<|fim_suffix|>**Fourth pass — the perm and tier.** Does this verb do anything dangerous? Is it a stable verb or an experimental one? Now you know whether to trust it in production.

**Fifth pass — the source.** Only if the previous four passes did not resolve your question. The source is the last resort.

Most of the time you will stop at the first or second pass. The doc and the contract together answer most questions.

## 2.16 The record is universal

Here is the important thing. Every verb has the same record shape.

Not almost every. Every.

`car` has the record. `map` has the record. `cortex/record` has the record. `composer/slider` has the record. `paint-dot` has the record. Every verb in every namespace in every module.

That uniformity is what makes introspection worth using. If you had to remember a different metadata shape for `card/*` verbs and another for `cortex/*` verbs and another for `composer/*` verbs, the mental overhead would defeat the purpose. Because the shape is universal, one skill — reading a verb record — works everywhere.

The uniformity is enforced at registration. `verbRegistry.js` normalizes every metadata blob to the same shape. Fields that were not passed are set to nil (or an empty list for lists). Fields that are unknown to the schema are dropped. The record you get from `help` is normalized; you do not have to worry about which module registered the verb.

## 2.17 Missing fields tell a story

<|fim_middle|>When a field is missing, that itself is information.

Missing `doc`: the verb author did not fill it in. This is a bug you can file. Every core verb should have a doc string.

Missing `contract`: same. Every verb should have a contract. If a verb takes complex arguments and the contract is missing, the reader has to guess from the examples.

Missing `examples`: this happens more often than it should. The training corpus wants examples on every verb. An empty examples field is a signal the verb has not been fully documented for pedagogical use.

Missing `source`: usually harmless. Some verbs are anonymous or generated. If the source is missing on a core verb, that is a bug.

Missing `since`: the verb is old and predates the since-tag convention, or the author forgot. Neither is critical; the field is advisory.

Missing `atom`: this is common and fine. Atoms are optional groupings.

Missing `namespace`: the verb is in the base. Not a bug.

<|fim_suffix|>If you see a lot of missing fields, the verb is not well documented. If you see all fields present, the verb is well documented. `help` gives you both signals in one pass.

## 2.18 The registry validation step

At startup, Motoi runs `validateRegistry` from `src/verbRegistry.js`. This walks every registered verb and checks a specific invariant: if a verb's name pattern suggests it changes state (ends in `!`, starts with `card-`, etc.) and the perm was inferred rather than explicitly declared, the validation fails and the runtime refuses to start.

Why this specific check? Because forgetting to declare a perm on a state-changing verb is the single most dangerous authoring mistake. A verb that looks like a write but was inferred as `read` slips past the dispatcher's perm gate. The startup validation catches this before any cart runs.

The check does not enforce anything else. It does not require doc strings, examples, contracts, since, or source. Those are cultural expectations, not runtime invariants. If you write a verb with a doc string of an empty string, the runtime will still start. If you skip the examples, the runtime will still start.

The consequence: the metadata layer is culturally load-bearing but not technically enforced. That trade is deliberate — a stricter validator would slow down authoring; a looser validator would let dangerous verbs ship. The dispatcher's perm check is the hard line; everything else is soft.

## 2.20 The record is the manual

The reference manual for Motoi is generated from the registry. `src/docs-emitter.js` walks every registered verb, reads the same record `help` returns, and emits a big SLAT file with a section per verb.

This means the reference manual has exactly the same information as `(help 'foo)`. There is no separate authoring pass. If a verb changes, the manual updates. If a verb is added, the manual grows. If a verb is removed, the manual shrinks. The manual and the runtime cannot disagree by construction.

That is worth pausing on. In most languages the reference manual is a separate artifact, maintained by a documentation team, that drifts from the code. In Motoi the manual *is* the code's metadata, rendered. There is nowhere for drift to hide.

The consequence for the reader: if you are looking something up in the manual, and the manual is silent, `(help 'foo)` in the REPL will also be silent. Not because the manual missed it — because the metadata is missing at registration. File a bug against the module that registered the verb, and the fix propagates to both.

## 2.21 The record and the LLM

The metadata record is also what Motoi Copilot was trained on.

Every verb's record — name, doc, contract, arity, examples — is a training sample. The model learned to generate calls to `car` by seeing the record's examples in context. It learned to reach for the right verb when a user describes an intent by having seen thousands of doc-string-to-call pairings.

This is why the doc string matters. A well-written doc string trains a well-behaved model. A vague or missing doc string produces a model that guesses. When you write a verb, you are writing training data. The kid who uses Motoi in five years will experience your verb through what the model learned from your metadata.

Chapter 13 comes back to this. The LLM-augmented verbs are grounded in the same registry the mechanical `help` reads from. Both surfaces — mechanical and modeled — depend on the same field set. Fill in the fields and both work.

## 2.26 Deep dive — the doc field style guide

The doc field is the field a reader touches first, so it deserves a longer look than the other fields got.

A good doc string in Motoi has three properties.

**Imperative mood.** \"Return the first element of a pair.\" Not \"Returns the first element\" or \"A function that returns the first element.\" The verb is a command the caller is issuing; the doc string describes the command in the same voice.

**One sentence.** If it does not fit in one sentence, it belongs in the reference manual's expanded description, not in the doc field. The doc string is what pops up under a REPL prompt in a hurry.

**No jargon that is not already in the reader's mouth.** A doc string that says \"Return the accumulator of a fold.\" is useless to a reader who does not know what a fold is. A doc string that says \"Combine a list into a single value by applying a two-argument procedure repeatedly.\" is useful to that same reader.

## 2.27 Deep dive — the contract mini-language

The contract field uses a small ad-hoc syntax to describe verb signatures. It is not a formal type system. It is a promise.

The core shapes are:

<|fim_middle|>- `number` — any number (integer or float)
- `integer` — an integer specifically
- `string` — a string
- `symbol` — a symbol
- `boolean` — a boolean
- `pair` — a pair
- `list` — a list
- `list-of-X` — a list whose elements are of type X
- `procedure` — a callable
- `any` — anything
<|fim_suffix|>- `nil` — the nil value

Composition:

- `(a b c) -> d` — takes a, b, c; returns d
- `(a b?)` — b is optional
- `(a ...)` — variadic in a
- `(:key val)` — a keyword-plist argument
- `X | Y` — union of X or Y
- `(-> X)` — a procedure that returns X (higher-order shape)

Examples from real Motoi verbs:

[type:fim] [source:book-chapter-code-block]

<|fim_prefix|>The contract is not typechecked at runtime. If a verb's contract says `(number) -> number` and you pass a string, you will get whatever the verb does with a string — probably an error, sometimes a coercion, occasionally a silent surprise.

The contract is useful because:

1. **It documents the intended shape.** A reader knows what to pass without having to run the verb.
2. **It documents the intended return.** A reader knows what they will get back without having to run the verb.
3. **It is what the LLM was trained on.** When the model generates code, the contract shapes what it generates.
4. **It is what a runtime-time checker could enforce.** Chapter 8 shows a `check-contract` macro that reads the contract field and enforces it if you want stricter semantics.
<|fim_middle|>
If you write a contract, keep it honest. If your verb accepts nil for the second argument, say `(a nil?)` not `(a b?)`. If your verb sometimes returns a symbol and sometimes returns a number, say `(a) -> symbol | number`, not `(a) -> any` — the honest union tells the reader more than the vague catch-all.

## 2.28 Deep dive — the examples field structure

The examples field is a list. Each element is a record with two keyword fields: `:level` and `:code`.

The `:level` is one of three symbols: `novice`, `intermediate`, `expert`. That vocabulary is closed; do not invent a fourth level.
<|fim_suffix|>
The `:code` is a string containing a runnable Scheme expression. Not a code block. Not a multi-line snippet with comments. One expression that a reader can copy, paste at the REPL, and see a result from.

Here is what the three levels are supposed to convey:

**Novice.** The verb used in isolation, with literal arguments. The reader can grasp the verb's shape from this single call. No auxiliary bindings, no composition with other verbs.

For `map`:

[type:fim] [source:book-chapter-code-block]

<|fim_prefix|>The three levels are a pedagogical arc. A reader who is unfamiliar reaches for novice. A reader who is fluent reaches for expert. A reader in the middle reaches for intermediate. Every verb should offer all three where possible.

Some verbs are too simple for three levels. `newline` is `(newline)` and that is all there is to say. In that case one novice example is enough, and the intermediate and expert slots may be empty.

<|fim_middle|>The examples are what feeds Motoi Copilot's training corpus most heavily. The doc string tells the model what the verb does; the examples show the model what a call *looks like*. Both together are what let the model generate a correct call when a user asks.

If you are running a stranger's cart in your runtime, you can enumerate every verb the cart calls and ask what perm tier each is. Any verb at `financial` or `personal-data` tier is a call you want to know about before you approve the cart.

<|fim_prefix|>Given a cart's form, `extract-verb-calls` walks the tree and returns every verb name. The filter keeps only the ones whose perm is in the sensitive list. You get back a list of the risky calls.

Motoi's sandbox uses this same logic. When a cart tries to run a `financial` verb, the dispatcher checks whether the cart's manifest declares that tier. If it does not, the call is refused. The perm field is the coordination point between the cart's manifest and the runtime's gate.

A verb at `perm: 'animate'` and `powerTier: 'animate'` is a motion verb that requires both permission and substrate power. If the substrate has thrown the animate power tier off (say, the tab is backgrounded), the verb is skipped even if perm would allow it.

Chapter 16 walks the sandbox layer in more depth. For this chapter, the takeaway is: the perm field is not decoration. It is the coordination point between authors, dispatchers, and sandboxes.

## 2.31 Deep dive — the tier field's roadmap

The tier field is `core`, `extended`, or `experimental`. But those are labels; what do they mean for the roadmap?

**Core.** Frozen. Never renaming. Never changing arity. The training corpus for Motoi Copilot depends on core verbs being stable across releases. If a core verb changes, the model has to be retrained. So they do not change.
<|fim_middle|>
The core set was frozen in July 2026 at 335 verbs (see `project_motoi_core_verbs_frozen_2026_07_16.md` in the memory notes). That set is what the model learned. Additions to core are rare and require Alfred's explicit approval.

**Extended.** Stable, but not yet trained on. Extended verbs may change name or arity between releases. Carts using extended verbs are advised to pin the runtime version.

Composer verbs (`composer/slider`, `composer/piano-roll`, etc.) are currently at `extended` tier. They will be promoted to `core` after the next training fold includes them.

**Experimental.** May change without notice. Do not build production carts on top of these. Reserved for verbs that are being prototyped and whose contract is still being worked out.

The LLM-augmented verbs from Chapter 13 (`what-is`, `explain`, `reason-about`) are at `experimental` tier while the LLM binding matures. They will be promoted after the ergonomics settle.

If you are auditing a cart for durability, count how many extended and experimental verbs it uses. A cart with only core verbs will survive any Motoi release. A cart with experimental verbs is a snapshot in time.

## 2.33 What the fields collectively enable

Take all eleven public fields together and you have enough to:

- Render a reference-manual entry
- Render a REPL help card
- Generate a training pair for the LLM
- Audit a cart's perm usage
- Group verbs by namespace or atom for a table of contents
- Filter verbs by tier for durability audits
- Filter verbs by since for release-note generation
- Point a reader to the source when the metadata is insufficient
- Enforce the contract at runtime if you wire in a checker
<|fim_middle|>
Every one of those uses reads from the same record. Every one of those uses is available to any programmer. There is no privileged tooling that has access to the record and no verb layer that does not.

This is what \"the record is universal\" means in practice. The universality is why the record is worth the field-by-field attention we gave it in this chapter.

## 2.34 A closing story

Here is a story from Motoi's development.

Early in the project the metadata records were partial. `car` had a doc string but no examples. `cons` had a contract but no arity. `cortex/record` had none of the above.

The introspection layer worked, but it worked half. `(help 'car)` returned a record with three of ten fields filled. `(help 'cons)` returned a record with two of ten. Programmers using the REPL got shrugs where they expected answers.

At some point Alfred pushed a rule: no verb ships without a full metadata record. Every registration call had to include doc, contract, arity, and at least one novice example. The registry validation was extended (informally at first) to nag on missing fields.

<|fim_suffix|>Within a week the introspection layer went from half-useful to fully useful. Every `(help ...)` call returned a complete record. The REPL felt different — questions had answers. The training corpus, when it was generated, had complete pairs on every verb.

The lesson: the metadata record is a discipline, not a feature. The runtime does not enforce it. The culture does. Every author who fills in the fields is contributing to a language that answers questions. Every author who skips the fields is contributing to a language that shrugs.

Fill in the fields. Every verb, every time. The reader on the other end will thank you.

## 3.3 The overlap — type-of on names vs values

Here is a subtlety worth calling out. `type-of` overlaps with the contract retrieval verb in a way that can confuse.

`(type-of 42)` returns `integer`. `(type-of 'foo)` returns `symbol`.
<|fim_middle|>
But `,type foo` at the REPL returns the *contract* of the verb named `foo`. Not `symbol`.

The two behaviors are different:

- **Value-side type-of**: takes a value, returns the runtime type symbol.
- **Verb-side type retrieval** (accessible via `,type` REPL command or `contract-of` verb): takes a name, returns the contract string.
<|fim_suffix|>
The REPL meta-command `,type` in `src/repl.js` uses `typeOf` from the introspection layer, which returns the contract. This is a naming inconsistency the language has lived with. The book distinguishes them:

- Use `type-of` in Scheme code for value inspection.
- Use `contract-of` (or `,type` at the REPL) for verb-signature inspection.

If you type `(type-of 'map)` at the REPL, what happens depends on whether you are treating `'map` as a symbol value (in which case `type-of` returns `symbol`) or as a verb name (in which case you probably meant `contract-of`).

## 3.7 The projection family

Together, the projection verbs are:

- `describe(name)` — verb name → paragraph
- `help(name)` — verb name → full record
<|fim_middle|>- `doc-of(name)` — verb name → doc string
- `contract-of(name)` — verb name → contract string
- `arity-of(name)` — verb name → arity value
- `source-of(name)` — verb name → source pointer
- `examples-of(name)` — verb name → list of example records
- `type-of(value)` — any value → runtime-type symbol
- `keys(hash)` — hash → list of keys
- `values(hash)` — hash → list of values
<|fim_suffix|>- `length(list-or-string)` — length as an integer
- `shape-of(value)` — value → composite description (Chapter 13, LLM-augmented)

That is the family. Each is a projection over the metadata or the runtime state. Each is one call. Each returns data.

Learn the projection verbs the way you would learn accessor methods in an object-oriented language. Once you have them memorized, the language becomes queryable at a rhythm faster than you can look things up in a manual.

A list of three integers might be an (x, y, z) coordinate. It might be an RGB color. It might be an image resolution. It might be a musical chord. The mechanical `type-of` and `length` will not distinguish.

<|fim_suffix|>For that you have three options:

1. **Look at the caller.** If the value came from `(color/from-rgb 128 64 32)`, it is a color. Read the source or the contract.

2. **Ask the LLM.** `shape-of` will guess based on context — if the surrounding code is drawing, the LLM will guess color; if it is playing audio, the LLM will guess chord.

3. **Use records instead of anonymous tuples.** If your data is going to be introspected, wrap it in a record with a type tag:

<|fim_prefix|>Now the meaning is baked into the value. `type-of` returns `record`, and `record-type` returns `color`. Any introspecting reader knows what they are looking at.

## 3.19 The three questions

There are three questions this chapter's verbs answer.
<|fim_suffix|>
**What is this name?** Use `describe` or `help`. Named things — verbs — are described by reading the metadata record.

**What is this value?** Use `type-of`, `length`, `keys`. Runtime values are inspected by asking the runtime what it holds.

**What does this verb expect?** Use `contract-of` or `arity-of`. The verb's signature is in the metadata; project the field you need.

Three questions. Six or seven verbs. Every question one verb call away.

## 3.23 Composing describe with mental models

There is a habit worth building.

When you learn a new verb, run `(describe 'new-verb)` immediately. Read the two-line output. That is your first mental model of the verb. Do not skip this step, even if you think you already know what the verb does.

Then look at the examples with `(examples-of 'new-verb)`. Read the novice, intermediate, and expert versions. That is your second mental model — how the verb is *used*, not just what it does.

Then, only then, use the verb. If it does what you expected, the mental model was right. If it surprises you, introspect the return value with `type-of` and `keys` and refine your model.
<|fim_middle|>
This four-step cycle — describe, examples, use, introspect — is how a Motoi programmer learns a verb. Repeat it a few dozen times and you have absorbed a serious chunk of the language.

## 3.24 A final observation

The projection verbs are small and cheap. Each takes one argument. Each returns one thing. Each is one line to call. Each composes with every other.

Because they are small and cheap, using them becomes reflexive. You do not think about calling `describe`; your fingers just type it. You do not think about running `type-of` on an uncertain value; your fingers just run it.

That reflex is the point. Introspection is not something you decide to do; it is something you do without deciding, dozens of times an hour, whenever a question arises. The projection verbs are the size and shape they are because they are meant to be reflexes.

## 3.27 Deep dive — the type vocabulary

The `type-of` return vocabulary is a closed set. Let me walk each one, since a reader who does not know what `char` or `port` looks like will have trouble reading later chapters.

**integer.** A whole number without decimal. `42`, `-7`, `0`. Motoi's integers are arbitrary-precision; you can compute `(expt 2 100)` and get back a real integer, not a wraparound.

**real.** A number with decimal. `3.14`, `-0.5`, `1.0`. Motoi's reals are IEEE 754 double-precision floating point. The float trap (Book of Values Chapter 6) applies.

**string.** A sequence of Unicode characters. `\"hello\"`, `\"日本語\"`. Strings are immutable.
<|fim_middle|>
**boolean.** `#t` or `#f`. Only these two values.

**symbol.** An interned atom. `'foo`, `'car`. Symbols compare by identity, not by name.

**char.** A single Unicode character. `#\\a`, `#\\space`, `#\\日`. Rare in user code; used in string manipulation.

**list.** A nil-terminated chain of pairs. `(1 2 3)`, `()`, `(a b c)`. The main sequence type.

**pair.** A cons cell with car and cdr. `(1 . 2)`. A list is a pair whose cdr is a list.

**nil.** The empty list, also the null value. There is only one nil.

**procedure.** A callable — a lambda, a defined function, a verb from the registry. All are procedures.

**vector.** A fixed-size indexed collection. `#(1 2 3)`. Mutable; index access is O(1).

<|fim_suffix|>**hash.** A key-value map. `(hash :a 1 :b 2)`. Motoi's default hash is unordered; ordered variants exist as separate types.

**record.** A tagged structure with named fields. `(make-record 'color :r 128 :g 64 :b 32)`. `record-type` returns the tag; `record-field` returns a specific field.

**error.** An error record with fields like `:message`, `:location`, `:stack`, `:cause`. Chapter 8 walks the shape.

**port.** An I/O handle — file, socket, string port. Rare in user code; used by verbs that read or write streams.

Fifteen types. That is the whole runtime vocabulary. Every value you will ever see in a Motoi program has one of these fifteen types.

If you see a `type-of` result that is not in the list, either the runtime added a type since this chapter was written, or you are in a dialect (Sakura, Lacuna) that added its own types. Motoi's base is fifteen.

## 3.35 A common question — why not just print?

A reader might ask: why not just `(display x)` and read the printed form?
<|fim_middle|>
Answer: because printing is lossy. A list of records prints as a nested s-expression that is hard to read for anything nontrivial. A hash prints as a flat kv-listing that loses structure. A procedure prints as `<fn>` with no signature. An error prints as a message but the fields are hidden.

Introspection is precise. Printing is a first-pass sanity check.

For simple values, printing is enough. `(display 42)` tells you 42. `(display \"hello\")` tells you hello. Fine.

For composite values — records, nested hashes, closures, errors — printing is a starting point but introspection is where you actually learn the shape. Reach for `type-of` and its friends after the first `display` gave you a shrug.

<|fim_suffix|>Chapter 4 will show how to reach the source pointer when even introspection is not enough, so you can go read the implementation. Introspection first; source-reading only when introspection runs out.

## 3.36 An educational aside — why the record fields have colons

You may have noticed that record field names have a leading colon: `:name`, `:age`. That is Motoi's keyword syntax.

A keyword is a self-evaluating symbol used as a field or parameter name. `:name` evaluates to itself; it does not need to be quoted. This makes keyword-plists (like `:subject 'user :predicate 'preferred-color`) easy to write — no quoting overhead.

`type-of` on a keyword returns `symbol`:

## 3.40 A closing observation about naming

The projection verbs are named for what they *return*, not for what they *take*. `type-of` returns the type. `arity-of` returns the arity. `doc-of` returns the doc. `source-of` returns the source.

<|fim_middle|>This is a small consistency but it helps memory. Once you know the naming convention, you can guess the projection verb for a field by adding `-of` to the field name.

Some exceptions: `describe` (not `paragraph-of`) because the return is a longer thing than one field. `help` (not `record-of`) because the return is the whole record. `keys` and `values` (not `keys-of` and `values-of`) because they are older Scheme conventions.

Motoi tried to be consistent; the exceptions are historical. Once you have used the family for a week, the naming feels natural.

## 3.46 The type vocabulary as a contract

<|fim_middle|>The fifteen-entry type vocabulary is itself a promise. When you write a contract that says `(list) -> integer`, the reader can be confident about what `list` means, because the vocabulary is fixed.

If Motoi's type system were open — if any code could invent new type tags — the contract mini-language would be less trustworthy. `(list) -> integer` might mean the list type Motoi ships with, or it might mean some user-defined list-like type. Ambiguity would creep in.

By closing the vocabulary, Motoi keeps contracts unambiguous. Every `list` in every contract in every verb means the same runtime type. Every `hash` means the same runtime hash. Every `record` means the same runtime record.

The trade-off is that Motoi cannot express types like \"a list whose elements are all colors.\" You would write that as `list` in the contract and use a predicate at runtime. The type system does not track element constraints.

<|fim_suffix|>For the size of language Motoi is, this trade is a good one. Full parametric types would triple the complexity of the introspection surface for a modest gain in expressiveness. The fifteen-entry vocabulary is small enough to keep in your head and expressive enough to describe most Motoi values.

## 3.49 Postscript — describe vs help, one more time

The distinction between `describe` and `help` is one of the most-asked questions from new Motoi programmers. Let me pin it down.

**describe** returns a string. Two lines. Formatted for humans. Meant for reading with your eyes at the REPL.

**help** returns a record. Ten fields. Formatted for programs. Meant for querying with other verbs.
<|fim_middle|>
Both read from the same underlying metadata. Both are cheap. Both are safe.

If you are at a REPL and want to know what a verb does, use `describe`. If you are in code and want to project a specific field or feed the record to another verb, use `help`.

The REPL meta-command `,help` uses a slightly different formatter (see `printHelp` in `src/repl.js`) that prints multiple lines with labels — the `printHelp` formatter is nicer than plain `describe` for terminal viewing, but the underlying data is the same record.

If in doubt, use `describe` for prose and `help` for data. That is the whole rule.

<|fim_suffix|>Every source pointer follows the format `path:line`. Path is relative to the runtime root. Line is 1-indexed.

Some examples of what to do with the pointer:

**Open in an editor.** If your editor supports `file:line` navigation (most do), you can copy-paste the pointer and jump straight to the implementation.

The source pointer is a bridge from the metadata layer to the source-code layer. Cross it when you need to; stay on the metadata side of the bridge most of the time.

## 4.7 The source-pointer drift problem

<|fim_middle|>As mentioned in Chapter 2, source pointers are manually maintained strings. If a verb's implementation moves within its file, the line number drifts.

There is no runtime check for drift. If a verb's `source` field says `src/base.js:73` and the actual implementation is at line 85, `source-of` will still return line 73. Following the pointer takes you to the wrong line.

Two mitigations:

1. **Search within the file.** Once you are in `src/base.js`, search for the verb name (`grep 'car'` or your editor's search) to find the actual current line.

<|fim_suffix|>2. **File a bug.** If you notice a drift, file it. The fix is a metadata update: change the `source` field in the registration call.

There is a planned auto-source-pointer feature (`engineering/AUTO-SOURCE-POINTERS.slat`, not yet landed) that would derive the source pointer from the JS stack trace at registration time. When that lands, drift will not be possible. Until then, treat source pointers as helpful-but-approximate.

## 4.8 What source-of does not do

`source-of` does not read the source. It returns the pointer.

If you want the source code itself, you need a separate file-reader verb. Motoi's `read-file` and `read-file-lines` verbs do this; combine them with `source-of` to get the code.

## 4.9 source-of and confidentiality

Some verbs deliberately have no source pointer. This is Chapter 16's topic, briefly previewed here.
<|fim_middle|>
A cart running in a sandboxed environment may not want to expose where its private verbs are implemented. The runtime can strip source pointers from the metadata before returning it to introspection callers. When it does, `source-of` returns nil.

This does not mean the verb has no source. It means the source is confidential. The introspection layer is telling you honestly: I know where this is, but I am not going to tell you.

<|fim_suffix|>The runtime's default is to expose source pointers for all core and extended verbs. Sandboxed runtimes may redact. If you see nil from `source-of` on a verb you know exists, either the field was never populated or the runtime is redacting.

Chapter 16 covers redaction policies in detail.

`examples-of` returns the tiered examples list from the metadata.

## 4.20 The three verbs and the workflow reflex

Chapter 3 named the introspection reflex — bind, type-of, project, recurse, decide. This chapter's verbs deepen it for names.

When you meet a verb name you do not recognize:

1. **doc-of** — what does it do?
2. **examples-of** — what does a call look like?
<|fim_middle|>3. **source-of** — if the above did not answer, where is it implemented?

Three verbs. In that order. Most of the time you stop at step 2. Sometimes you go to step 3.

Practice this reflex a hundred times and it becomes automatic. Every unfamiliar verb, you type `(doc-of 'name)` before you type anything else. Every doc you read, you follow up with `(examples-of 'name)` to see the shape of a call. Every impenetrable verb, you fall back to `(source-of 'name)` and read the source.

The three verbs are small. The reflex they enable is large.

## 4.21 An honest observation about source-reading

Source-reading is a skill separate from introspection. Motoi's introspection layer minimizes the need for it, but does not eliminate it.

<|fim_suffix|>Some things you can only learn from source:

- The exact implementation strategy (stable vs unstable sort, iterative vs recursive impl)
- The performance characteristics (O(n) vs O(n log n) vs O(1))
- The edge case handling (what happens when the input is empty, or nil, or malformed)
- The interaction with the runtime (what globals it reads, what caches it uses)

For these questions the metadata is not enough. The doc string can hint (\"stable sort\") but cannot spell out the details. The source is authoritative.

If you find yourself reading source often, that is a signal the metadata layer is under-serving you. Consider filing bugs on verbs where the metadata was insufficient. Motoi wants source-reading to be rare; a verb whose metadata forces frequent source-reading is a candidate for better docs.

## 4.25 Deep dive — the doc-string style

I want to spend a section on doc-string style, because you will register your own verbs eventually and the style guide matters.

A doc-string in Motoi is:

- One sentence. Two if the first cannot stand alone.
- Imperative mood. \"Return the first element\" not \"Returns the first element\" or \"A function that returns...\"
- No jargon that is not already in the reader's mouth.
- Names the keyword arguments if the verb has any: \"Kwargs: :subject :predicate :object\".
- Ends with a period.

Some good examples:

<|repo_name|>motoi-scheme<|file_sep|>scheme-books/book-of-introspection/04-docof-sourceof.book.slatl
[type:fim] [source:book-chapter-code-block]

<|fim_prefix|>Not a sentence. Not imperative. No period. Zero information.

The three-property test: imperative, one sentence, no unfamiliar jargon. Apply it to every doc-string you write. If it fails, rewrite until it passes.

## 4.26 Deep dive — the source pointer format

The source pointer is `path:line`. That is the format. No other punctuation, no offsets, no character positions.

<|fim_middle|>Some conventions:

- Path is always relative to the repo root, not absolute.
- Line is the line where the registration call starts, not where the impl function starts.
- If the verb is defined and registered in different places, prefer the registration site.
- If the pointer would be ambiguous (multiple registrations of the same verb), prefer the canonical one and mark the others as deprecated aliases.

The pointer is a hint for a human reader. It does not need to be precise to the character. If the reader gets to the right file and within ten lines of the right position, the pointer has done its job.
<|fim_suffix|>
## 4.27 Deep dive — the examples list schema

Each example is a record with two fields: `:level` and `:code`.

`:level` is a symbol. The valid values are `novice`, `intermediate`, `expert`. Case matters; use lowercase symbols.

`:code` is a string. The string must contain a runnable Scheme expression — no comments, no multi-line explanations, no ellipses. If you cannot fit the example on one line, wrap the parts in a `begin`:

## 4.35 A note on the specialized projections vs help

There are two ways to read a specific field. You can call the specialized projection verb (`doc-of`, `source-of`, `examples-of`) or you can call `help` and pull the field out yourself.

<|repo_name|>motoi-scheme<|file_sep|>scheme-books/book-of-introspection/04-docof-sourceof.book.slatl
[type:fim] [source:book-chapter-code-block]

<|fim_prefix|>Option A is shorter, faster to type, and more idiomatic. Option B is more general — you can extract any field, not just the ones with specialized projections.

The rule of thumb: if there is a specialized projection, use it. If you need a field that has no specialized projection, use `help` and pull the field out. Motoi ships specialized projections for the fields that are used most often; the rest live only on the record.

Fields with specialized projections:
- `doc` — `doc-of`
- `source` — `source-of`
- `examples` — `examples-of`
<|fim_middle|>- `contract` — `contract-of` (aka `type-of` at the REPL)
- `arity` — `arity-of`

Fields without specialized projections (use `help`):
- `namespace`
- `tier`
- `perm`
- `atom`
<|fim_suffix|>- `since`
- Dispatcher-only fields

The lack of a specialized projection is not a bug — it reflects usage frequency. If a field becomes commonly-projected, adding a specialized verb is a five-line change.

<|fim_middle|>## 15.24 One final observation

Performance introspection is one of the areas where Motoi's small design pays off. Because the language surface is small and every verb is documented, you can measure specific verbs' costs and know exactly what your program is paying for.

Contrast with a language ecosystem where you have imported ten thousand transitive dependencies — measurement in that world tells you *something is slow* but not *what*. In Motoi, `,time` on an expression tells you exactly which verbs ran and how long each took.

<|fim_suffix|>Small language, precise measurement. That is the payoff.

## 15.30 Deep-seed — the runtime performance model

Motoi's evaluator is a tree-walking interpreter. It is not optimized for raw throughput. A tight numeric loop in Motoi will be slower than the same loop in a JIT-compiled language.

This is a deliberate design choice. Motoi trades throughput for uniformity. Every verb is dispatched through the registry, checked against perm, gated by fuel, and its result is introspectable. That uniformity has a cost.

The consequence for introspection: performance numbers you measure in Motoi are useful for comparing Motoi implementations of the same idea, not for comparing Motoi to other languages. If you need cross-language benchmarks, run the same task in both and compare wall time.

## 15.31 Deep-seed — cross-runtime consistency

<|fim_suffix|>Different Motoi runtimes may have different performance profiles. A Node.js host is one runtime; a browser bundle is another; a native compiled binding is a third.

Performance introspection numbers are per-runtime. `,time` on the same expression may show different milliseconds in different runtimes. Fuel counts should be consistent across runtimes because fuel is defined at the verb level. Memory reporting depends on the host's GC.

When you publish benchmark results, note the runtime. `(:runtime \"node-20\" :ms 234)`. That way anyone reading can reproduce.

  (cond
    ((string? x) x)
    ((symbol? x) (symbol->string x))
    ((number? x) (number->string x))
    (else (with-output-to-string (lambda () (display x))))))

(define (format-verb-info meta name-str)
<|fim_middle|>  (if (not meta)

            (contract (or (cdr (assoc 'contract meta)) \"(no contract)\"))
            (arity (or (cdr (assoc 'arity meta)) \"(no arity)\"))
            (first-example
             (let ((exs (cdr (assoc 'examples meta))))
               (and exs (not (null? exs))
                    (cdr (assoc :code (car exs)))))))
        (string-append
          name \" — \" doc \"\\n\"
          \"contract: \" contract \"\\n\"
          \"arity:    \" (any->string arity) \"\\n\"
<|fim_suffix|>          (if first-example
              (string-append \"example:  \" first-example)
              \"\")))))

(define my-help-command
  (lambda (ctx argv)
    (let ((name (car argv)))
      (if (not name)
          (ctx-output ctx \"usage: ,my-help <verb>\")
          (ctx-output ctx (format-verb-info (help name) name))))))

## C.26 The extensibility principle

Every layer of Motoi is extensible via the same pattern: query primitives, format the result, register the extension. The REPL is the most visible example, but the same pattern works for:

- Reference-manual renderers (query registry, emit SLAT sections)
- Cart audit tools (query cart, check against registry)
<|fim_middle|>- Runtime dashboards (query state, format as UI)
- Training-corpus generators (query registry, emit training pairs)

Every one of these is a Scheme program. Every one uses the introspection primitives. Every one is customizable by rewriting the format-and-register logic.

## C.27 A final observation

Motoi's introspection layer is not designed just for reading. It is designed for building. The primitives are meant to be composed into tools. The reference REPL is an example, not a limit.
<|fim_suffix|>
Write your own tools. That is what the primitives are for.

<|fim_prefix|>`car` is the first element. `cdr` (say \"could-er\") is everything after the first. `cons` prepends. These names are old and they stick around because they are short and every Lisper knows them.

The performance tradeoff:

<|fim_middle|>- Prepending to a Motoi list is O(1). Prepending to a Python list is O(n).
- Indexing into a Motoi list is O(n). Indexing into a Python list is O(1).
- Iterating is O(n) in both.
- The Motoi list is *persistent* — the old list is unchanged when you `cons` onto it. Python's list is mutable, so `xs.append(6)` changes `xs` in place.
<|fim_suffix|>
Different tools. If you find yourself indexing a lot, you either use `list-ref` (which is O(n) and honest about it) or you reach for a different structure. Motoi has hash tables, association lists, and — via modules — vectors and arrays. Lists are the default because they are cheap to build and destructure, and because pattern-matching on `(cons head tail)` is one of the most useful moves in the language.

**Higher-order stuff.** This is where Motoi has genuinely nicer ergonomics than Python.

## 2.5 Async and await

JavaScript's async story is `Promise`, `async`, `await`, and an event loop that runs promise resolutions between synchronous chunks.

<|fim_middle|>Motoi's answer is different in shape. There are three tools:

1. **First-class continuations** (`call/cc`). You can capture the rest of the computation as a function and call it later. This is a superpower and a hazard; most programs never use it directly.
2. **Delimited continuations and generators** (via a module). If you want the shape of `async function* () { yield await ...; }`, this is where it lives.
3. **Channels and lightweight processes** (via a module). If your program is coordinating many concurrent things, you spin up processes that talk over channels.

<|fim_suffix|>At the base level, Motoi is synchronous. If you're writing a script or a game or a simulation, you write it straight through. If you're writing a server or a UI that must coordinate many things, you reach for the concurrency module.

The important shift from JavaScript: in JavaScript, *anything can be async*, and once one function is async everything that calls it becomes async, and this colors your entire codebase. In Motoi, async is opt-in and scoped. Most of your code stays synchronous. This is a different tradeoff than JavaScript's; it fits differently-shaped problems.

## 2.10 The DOM, or lack thereof

JavaScript has the DOM. Motoi does not. When you want to draw things, Motoi has a framebuffer and drawing verbs — pixels, sprites, text, shapes. When you want sound, Motoi has audio verbs — tones, notes, kits. When you want interaction, Motoi has a game loop with `big-bang` semantics inherited from a long tradition of teaching languages.

If your problem is *build a web UI*, JavaScript is right. If your problem is *build a small program that draws and makes sound and reacts to input*, Motoi has a shorter path.

## 2.11 The type situation

JavaScript is dynamically typed with runtime coercion (`\"3\" + 4 === \"34\"`, `\"3\" - 4 === -1`, and other party tricks). TypeScript layers static types on top.

Motoi is dynamically typed *without* the coercion. `+` on a number and a string is an error. `=` on two different types is `#f`. Types are checked lazily at the operation, and errors say what went wrong.

There is no TypeScript-for-Motoi. There is a gradual-typing story via contracts, in a module. Most Motoi code uses no types at all and gets by on tests and predicates like `number?`, `string?`, `list?`.
<|fim_middle|>
If you have PTSD from `undefined` being passed silently through eight layers of your code before exploding — Motoi is a relief. There is no `undefined`. There is a symbol you can name (`'undefined`) if you want one, but it's a symbol, not a value that arrives out of nowhere.

## 2.12 npm-scale ecosystem

JavaScript has millions of packages. Motoi has ~40 modules today.

This is a real difference. If you need to talk to Stripe or send an email or parse a specific proprietary binary format, JavaScript has a battle-tested library and Motoi does not. For those tasks, use JavaScript.

Motoi's smallness is a feature for the class of problems where you *don't* want a hundred dependencies for a simple thing. If your program is a game, a simulation, a small tool, a language experiment, a piece of teaching material — Motoi's smallness is a gift. If your program is a service that has to speak twenty protocols, Motoi will bite you.

Pick right for the shape.

## 2.13 Why you might pick Motoi over JavaScript

- You want closures and first-class functions without the surrounding syntax noise.
- You want lists that are structurally persistent by default.
<|fim_suffix|>- You want tail-call elimination as a guarantee.
- You want macros — real macros, not template strings.
- You want a small language you can read end-to-end.
- You want to write DSLs.

Why you might stay with JavaScript:

- You are shipping to a browser.
- You need one of the many mature npm libraries.
- Your team knows JavaScript.
- Your problem is a normal web-service or web-UI shape.

Both languages are honest choices. This book gives you the vocabulary to move between them.

## 3.12 Concurrency

This is where the languages diverge sharply.

Clojure's story is *identities and values*: atoms, refs, agents. It runs on the JVM which gives you native threads, and its data structures are thread-safe by construction.

<|fim_suffix|>Lua's rule: only `false` and `nil` are falsy. Every other value (including `0`, `\"\"`, empty tables) is truthy.

## 4.6 The `nil` problem, or lack of it

Lua's `nil` is the language's biggest source of pain. `nil` in a table means \"this key is absent.\" `nil` as a function argument can mean \"you didn't pass one\" or \"you passed nil deliberately.\" `nil` as a return value collapses variadic returns silently. `nil`-holes in arrays break `#t`.

<|fim_middle|>Motoi doesn't have `nil` in this sense. It has:

- `#f`, the boolean false.
- `'()`, the empty list.
- Absence in a lookup returns `#f` explicitly (`assoc` returns `#f` when not found).
- There is no *value* that means \"absent\" — absence is a return-value contract.
<|fim_suffix|>
You will not have Lua-style nil bugs. You may still have bugs — Motoi is dynamic, so wrong-type errors are runtime. But you will not have the specific class of bug that comes from `nil` being both a value and an absence.

## 5.2 The type system, up front

Java is statically typed with inference in some places (`var`) and explicit typing in most. Motoi is dynamically typed. This is the biggest single difference between the two languages, and colors everything else.

**What you lose moving from Java to Motoi:**

- Compile-time errors for type mismatches. Motoi's errors happen at runtime.
<|fim_middle|>- IDE-driven autocompletion by type. Motoi's completion is by verb name.
- The compiler as a *co-designer* — Java lets you sketch a class signature and get told everywhere your program doesn't fit yet.
- Refactoring tools that know how types flow.

**What you gain:**

- Small, expressive code.
- No boilerplate type annotations.
- Values-first thinking: a list is a list, whatever it holds; a function is a function, whatever it maps.
<|fim_suffix|>- Fast prototyping — a Motoi REPL session grows into a program without ever writing a `class`.

If your work is *building a durable large-team codebase over years*, Java's type system is a load-bearing beam. If your work is *exploring an idea, building a small program, teaching, prototyping*, Motoi's absence of types is a relief.

You can adopt a middle ground: Motoi has a contracts module. You can annotate function boundaries with predicates that check at runtime. Not the same as static types. Catches some of the same bugs, differently.

## 5.10 Concurrency

Java has native threads, synchronized methods, `java.util.concurrent`, `ExecutorService`, `CompletableFuture`, virtual threads (project Loom). It is a *deep* concurrency story.

Motoi's core is single-threaded. Concurrency lives in a module and models channels + processes, closer to Erlang or Go.

For your typical Motoi program — a game, a small server, a script — single-threaded is fine. For the class of program where Java's concurrency shines — a service handling many thousands of concurrent connections with fine-grained locking — Motoi is not the right tool.

Pick what fits your problem.

<|fim_middle|>## 5.11 Build and deployment

Java has Maven, Gradle, an ecosystem of build tools older than some of the programmers reading this. It has a huge library index (Maven Central). It has predictable production deployment: build a JAR, run the JAR, done.

Motoi has a single interpreter binary and a directory of `.scm` files. No build step. No packaging beyond \"put the files somewhere the interpreter can find them.\" This is a strength for small projects and a limitation for large teams that want reproducible builds and stable versioned dependencies.

## 5.12 Why you might pick Motoi over Java

- You are building something small, prototypal, or explorative.
- You want no build step.
- You want to write DSLs and macros without dropping into a separate metaprogramming system.
- You want a language a kid could learn to write in a weekend.
- You want the fantasy-console kit.

<|fim_suffix|>Why you might stay with Java:

- You have an enterprise team of thirty developers.
- You need mature libraries (databases, HTTP, serialization).
- You need production-grade concurrency on many cores.
- You need the compile-time safety guarantees of static types.
- You need the JVM ecosystem — Spring, Micronaut, whatever.

Java and Motoi answer different questions. Java answers: *how do many people build one large durable system together?* Motoi answers: *how does one person build a small, expressive, complete thing?*

Both are honest questions.

## 6.2 The ownership question

Rust's ownership model is the language's defining feature. Every value has one owner. Moving transfers ownership; borrowing lends a reference; the borrow checker verifies safety at compile time.
<|fim_middle|>
Motoi has *none* of this. All values are garbage-collected. Multiple references to the same list are fine. Mutation happens by copying (functional idiom) or by `set!` (explicit).

There is nothing to translate here. Rust's ownership is a *design constraint* that shapes how you write; Motoi lets you ignore memory and pays for that with GC pauses. The two languages solve genuinely different problems.

<|fim_suffix|>What a Rust programmer can *use* from this observation: writing a small tool in Motoi is faster than writing it in Rust, because you don't fight the borrow checker. If the tool's runtime cost doesn't matter and correctness comes from types you can't have, Motoi's cost is minor. If it matters, Rust.

## 6.8 Concurrency

Rust: `std::thread`, `async`/`.await`, `tokio`, channels via `mpsc`, `Arc<Mutex<T>>`, `Send`/`Sync` traits enforced by the compiler.

Motoi: single-threaded core. Concurrency module provides channels + processes, closer to Go or Erlang.

Rust's `Send + Sync` is a compile-time guarantee that a value can safely cross thread boundaries. Motoi has no equivalent because Motoi's core has no threads.

For CPU-bound parallel work, Rust wins outright. For coordination-shaped concurrency (many things reacting to events, actor systems, game entities), Motoi's channel model is comfortable.

## 6.9 The macro comparison

Both languages have real macros. Rust's macros come in two flavors:

- `macro_rules!` — pattern-based, hygienic, like `syntax-rules`.
- Procedural macros — arbitrary compile-time code, like `syntax-case`.

<|fim_middle|>Motoi's core has `syntax-rules`; the module system provides `syntax-case`. Chapter 11 dives in.

The difference in *feel*: Rust's macros expand into token trees checked by the compiler. Motoi's macros expand into s-expressions evaluated at runtime. Rust's macros compose with the type system; Motoi's compose with the value system. Both are powerful in their own ways.

## 6.10 Zero-cost abstractions

Rust's guiding principle: abstractions should compile away to the same code you'd write by hand. `iter().filter().map().sum()` compiles to a tight loop.

Motoi does not make this promise. Every `map` allocates a new list. Every `filter` walks and filters. Every closure captures its environment. Interpretation has overhead the compiler cannot remove.

For hot code where nanoseconds matter, Motoi is not the tool. For most code — where a program runs once per keystroke or once per frame or once per network request — the overhead is invisible.

## 6.11 Ecosystem and tooling

Rust has cargo, clippy, rustfmt, a good LSP, crates.io with tens of thousands of packages, integration with many editors.

Motoi has bin/motoi (the interpreter/REPL/formatter), a reference manual, and a small set of modules.

This is a real gap. For anything involving external systems — HTTP clients, database drivers, cryptography libraries — Rust's ecosystem is where the work has been done.
<|fim_suffix|>
## 6.12 Why you might pick Motoi for something Rust-adjacent

- Prototyping the algorithm before writing the Rust.
- Writing a DSL that emits Rust code.
- Writing a build script or tool that shouldn't be in Rust.
- Writing the game logic (Motoi) while Rust handles the engine.
- Teaching functional programming ideas that Rust also uses.

Why you stay in Rust:

- Anything performance-sensitive.
- Anything memory-constrained.
- Anything security-sensitive at the systems level.
- Anything you plan to ship as a binary with no interpreter.

Rust and Motoi don't compete. They live in different neighborhoods.

## 7.10 The `nil` question

Ruby's `nil` is not as painful as Lua's, because Ruby is strict about `nil.method` throwing rather than returning `nil`. It's still a value that can flow through your program silently.

Motoi's `#f`/`'()` split (empty list vs boolean false) is a cleaner design. There is no `nil`. Absence is a return-value convention (`assoc` returns `#f` when absent) and the empty list is `'()`, which is not equal to `#f`.

## 7.11 Performance

Ruby has YJIT and TruffleRuby and various runtime speedups; it is not as slow as it once was, but it is not fast by systems-language standards. Motoi is an interpreter written in JavaScript. It is not fast either.

For most work — scripts, tools, small applications, games — both are fast enough. For compute-heavy work, both hand off to native (Ruby's C extensions, Motoi's host-language operations).

- Rails. Full stop, for many teams.
- The gem ecosystem is enormous and well-maintained.
- Blocks and method-chaining read like English in a way Motoi doesn't try to.
- Your team knows Ruby.

## 9.6 Types, or their absence

This is where Haskell and Motoi disagree loudest.

<|fim_middle|>Haskell's type system — algebraic data types, type classes, higher-kinded types, functional dependencies, GADTs, kind polymorphism — is a large, careful, load-bearing part of the language. `Maybe`, `Either`, `IO`, `State`, `Reader`, `Writer` — the whole scaffolding is types.

Motoi has none of that. Values are values. Functions are functions. There is no `Maybe a` — there is `#f` for absent and a value for present, and you check with `if`. There is no `Either` — there is a tagged list `('ok x)` or `('err msg)`. There is no `IO` — there is `display` and `read`, and they happen when you call them.

This is a massive tradeoff. Haskell's type system catches enormous classes of bug at compile time. Motoi catches nothing at compile time and finds those bugs at runtime, or via tests, or not at all.

<|fim_suffix|>There is no elegant answer to \"how do I get Haskell's safety in Motoi.\" You don't. You write more tests, you use contracts at boundaries, and you accept the risk.

The compensation is that Motoi programs are shorter, more experimental, and don't require the type-tetris-that-passes-and-then-runs feeling. Different tools.

Haskell's `IO`, `Maybe`, `State`, `List`, `Reader`, `Writer`, `STM` — all monads. Do-notation makes them read imperatively:

If your love of Haskell is monadic composition and do-notation, Motoi will feel like you're back in the wild. The compensation: most Motoi programs never need to reify \"the shape of sequenced effects\" because effects just happen when you call them.

## 9.10 Concurrency

Haskell has STM (software transactional memory), which is one of the language's best inventions. `TVar` + `atomically` gives you composable concurrent transactions. This is genuinely better than most languages' concurrency stories for a range of problems.

Motoi has channels + processes, closer to Erlang. No STM. If your concurrency needs are STM-shaped (many contending transactions on shared state), Haskell is right.

## 9.11 The ecosystem

Haskell's ecosystem is niche but deep — Hackage has excellent libraries for parsing, web serving, cryptography, and mathematical work. GHC is a serious compiler. Cabal and Stack solve build problems.
<|fim_middle|>
Motoi's ecosystem is small — a handful of first-party modules and a growing base.

## 9.12 Why you might pick Motoi over Haskell

- You want a REPL loop where you can throw code and get answers.
- You want to write DSLs via macros (Motoi's macros are simpler and more direct than Template Haskell).
- You want to avoid the type-tetris-until-it-compiles feeling.
- You want a language that starts fast and stays small.
- You want the fantasy-console kit.

(define kick-pattern  '(k - - - k - - - k - - - k - - -))
(define snare-pattern '(- - - - s - - - - - - - s - - -))
(define hat-pattern   '(h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h h))

;; --- melody (in semitones from A4) ---
(define riff '(-5 -3 0 -3 -5 -3 -5 -3 -7 -5 -3 -5 -7 -5 -3 -5))

  (unless (eq? step '-) (audio-fn)))

  (for-each (lambda (step) (play-step audio-fn step)) pattern))

;; --- one bar of everything ---
(define (bar visualize)
  ;; drums
  (for-each
    (lambda (i)
      (let ((k (list-ref kick-pattern i))
            (s (list-ref snare-pattern i))
            (h (list-ref hat-pattern i))
            (note (list-ref riff (modulo i 16))))
        ;; play each layer
        (unless (eq? k '-) (synth/kit 'kick 0))
        (unless (eq? s '-) (synth/kit 'snare 0))
        (unless (eq? h '-) (synth/kit 'hat 0))
        (audio/play 'tone (note->freq note) 0.11 'square)
        ;; visualize
        (when visualize
<|fim_suffix|>          (fb/clear 1)                          ; dark blue background
          (fb/circle 64 64 (if (eq? k '-) 20 40) 8)        ; kick pulse
          (when (not (eq? s '-))
            (fb/rect 10 30 108 60 7))                       ; snare flash
          (fb/pixel (modulo (+ i 32) 128) 64 10))))         ; hat spark

(define (iota n) (let loop ((i 0)) (if (= i n) '() (cons i (loop (+ i 1))))))

;; --- structure: intro, verse, verse, breakdown, verse ---
(define (demo)
  (bar #t)     ; intro bar with visuals
  (bar #t)     ; second intro
  (bar #t)     ; verse
  (bar #t)     ; verse
  (audio/halt) ; breakdown — silence
  (bar #t)     ; return
  (bar #t))    ; final

## 18.8 The cart file format

A Motoi cart is a `.scm` file. Convention — not enforcement — is that carts start with a small header comment naming the cart and crediting the author, then define state at the top, install callbacks in the middle, and end with `(render)` or nothing at all (the display driver pumps `on-frame` on its own in the REPL).

### 4.5 — Lua tables ↔ Sakura hash-tables

<|fim_suffix|>Lua tables serve two purposes: array-shape (`t[1], t[2], ...`) and dict-shape (`t.name, t.age`). In Motoi Scheme those are two data structures — `list` (or `vector`) for the array-shape and `hash-table` for the dict.

The color model differs: TIC-80 hard-codes a 16-color palette; Motoi Scheme carries a palette per session, defaults to a 16-color set drawn from a curated theme, and lets you swap palettes via a config field (`theme:` in `config.slat`).

### 4.8 — Anonymous functions

<|fim_middle|>Fennel `(fn [x] (+ x 1))` is Sakura `(lambda (x) (+ x 1))`. Same shape.

Clojure `#(+ % 1)` is Sakura `(lambda (x) (+ x 1))`. There's no built-in `#(...)` reader macro in the base; if you want one, `define-syntax` will get you a decent approximation but the general case (multi-argument `%1`, `%2`, `%3`) is more work than it's worth. <|fim_prefix|>But be aware: this is a subtle interaction with `set!` on the outer `x`. Read carefully if you nest deeply.

### The reader auto-quotes shape heads

At the REPL, `(circle 40 40 15)` isn't a call — the reader sees an unbound head and auto-quotes it. So the value is the tagged list `(circle 40 40 15)`. Then the display layer notices the shape and renders it.

This is *only* for shape heads: `circle`, `disc`, `line`, `rect`, `shapes`, `plot`. Everything else is a normal call. If you accidentally shadow one of those names, the auto-quote goes away for that name. If you want an unambiguous read, quote explicitly: `'(circle 40 40 15)`.
<|fim_middle|>
The rule is in `src/repl/repl.js` — `AUTO_QUOTE_HEADS`.

### Zero-indexing everywhere

Lua indexes from 1. Fennel too (it's a Lua transpiler). Motoi Scheme indexes from 0. `(list-ref xs 0)` is the first element.

<|fim_suffix|>### Numbers

Motoi Scheme distinguishes exact and inexact numbers, R7RS-style. `1/3` is exact; `0.3333` is inexact. Most arithmetic between exacts stays exact — `(+ 1/3 1/6)` is `1/2`. As soon as an inexact enters, everything becomes inexact — `(+ 1/3 0.5)` is `0.8333...`. If you're used to Lua's one-number-type simplicity, you can force inexact with `exact->inexact`.

  (let* ((snake (hash-ref s 'snake))
         (dir   (hash-ref s 'dir))

<|fim_prefix|>;; Summit: a D₆ rosette with a seed curve (a small arc).

(define seed-curve
<|fim_middle|>  (let ((t-vals (map (lambda (i) (/ i 10.0)) (math/array 0 10))))
    (map (lambda (t)
           (geom/point (* 3 t) (* 1 t)))
         t-vals)))

  (map (lambda (k)

                    (geom/point
                      (- (* x (geom/cos angle)) (* y (geom/sin angle)))
<|fim_suffix|>                      (+ (* x (geom/sin angle)) (* y (geom/cos angle))))))
                seed-curve)))
       (math/array 0 5)))

(define plot-data
  (map (lambda (curve)
         (plot/line curve))
       rotated-curves))

(define (nim-game-tree heaps depth)

      (let* ((nim-sum (game/nim-sum heaps))

<|fim_middle|>                      (if (>= i (length heaps))

                                                                             (if (= j i) (- h t) h))
<|fim_suffix|>                                                                           (comb/range 0 (length heaps))
                                                                           heaps)))
                                                       (list 'pile i 'take t 'result new-heaps)))
                                                   takes)))))))
             (children (map (lambda (move)
                              (nim-game-tree (cadr (assoc 'result move)) (- depth 1)))
                            moves)))
        (list 'heaps heaps 'nim-sum nim-sum 'outcome outcome 'depth depth 'children children))))

[type:fim] [source:book-chapter-code-block]

<|fim_prefix|>;; Define a 2×2 matrix (not a simple diagonal or rotation — something with clear eigenstructure)
(define A (matrix/make (list (list 3 1)
                              (list 1 3))))

;; Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors
(define evals (linalg/eigenvalues A))
(define evecs-result (linalg/eigenvectors A))

;; Generate a grid of points in the unit square
(define grid-points
  (let loop ((i 0) (acc '()))
    (if (> i 10)
        acc
        (let loop-j ((j 0) (acc2 acc))
          (if (> j 10)
              (loop (+ i 1) acc2)
              (loop-j (+ j 1)
                      (cons (list (/ i 10.0) (/ j 10.0)) acc2)))))))

;; Transform each point by A
<|fim_middle|>(define transform-point
  (lambda (p)
    (let ((v (matrix/make (list (list (car p)) (list (cadr p))))))
      (let ((result (matrix/* A v)))
        ;; Extract coordinates from the 2×1 matrix
        (list (matrix/ref result 0 0)
              (matrix/ref result 1 0))))))

(define transformed-grid (map transform-point grid-points))

;; Prepare to plot: original grid as blue dots, transformed grid as red dots
;; We'll use plot/scatter twice and overlay them, and also draw the eigenvectors as lines.

(define original-plot
  (plot/scatter
   (map car grid-points)
   (map cadr grid-points)
   (list (cons 'color \"blue\") (cons 'label \"Original\"))))

(define transformed-plot
<|fim_suffix|>  (plot/scatter
   (map car transformed-grid)
   (map cadr transformed-grid)
   (list (cons 'color \"red\") (cons 'label \"Transformed\"))))

;; Eigenvectors (assuming evecs-result is a list of two 2D vectors)
;; We'll draw them as arrows from the origin.
;; (For this example, we'll note them conceptually and include them in the plot description.)

(define combined-plot
  (plot/with
   (list original-plot transformed-plot)
   (list (cons 'title \"Transformation by A: Original (blue) vs Transformed (red)\")
         (cons 'width 600)
         (cons 'height 600))))

(list 'A A
      'eigenvalues evals
      'eigenvectors evecs-result
      'plot combined-plot)

<|fim_prefix|>;; Summit Artifact: Factor Tree Visualization

(define (smallest-prime-factor n)
  (define (try d)
    (cond
      ((> (* d d) n) n)
      ((= (modulo n d) 0) d)
      (else (try (+ d 1)))))
  (if (< n 2) 'nan (try 2)))

(define (prime? n)
  (and (> n 1) (= (smallest-prime-factor n) n)))

(define (factor-tree n)
<|fim_middle|>  (if (prime? n)
      n
      (let ((p (smallest-prime-factor n)))
        (list n (factor-tree p) (factor-tree (/ n p))))))

(define (layout-tree tree x y dx dy)
  (if (number? tree)
      (list (list 'node tree x y))
      (let* ((n (car tree))
             (left (cadr tree))
             (right (caddr tree))
             (left-x (- x dx))
             (right-x (+ x dx))
             (child-y (+ y dy)))
<|fim_suffix|>        (cons (list 'node n x y)
              (append
               (cons (list 'edge x y left-x child-y)
                     (layout-tree left left-x child-y (/ dx 2) dy))
               (cons (list 'edge x y right-x child-y)
                     (layout-tree right right-x child-y (/ dx 2) dy)))))))

(define (draw-factor-tree n)
  ;; Compute layout, return drawing commands.
  (let ((elements (layout-tree (factor-tree n) 48 4 20 10)))
    (list 'factor-tree-of n 'elements elements)))

;; Draw the factor tree of 60.
(draw-factor-tree 60)

            (list (cons 'title \"Equivalent Fractions: 1/2, 2/4, 4/8\"))))

(define x-coord (exact/rat 5 2))   ; 5/2 = 2.5
(define y-coord (exact/rat 7 3))   ; 7/3 ≈ 2.333...

  (plot/scatter
   (list (list (exact/->float x-coord) (exact/->float y-coord)))
   (list (cons 'title \"Point (5/2, 7/3) on the Coordinate Plane\"))))

(print \"  y = \" (exact/->string y-coord) \" = \" (exact/->float y-coord))

  ;; At least two of the four must be non-'nan
  (let* ((angle-rad (if (eq? angle-deg 'nan)
                        'nan
                        (geom/->radians angle-deg)))
         (new-hyp (cond
                    ((and (not (eq? opp 'nan)) (not (eq? angle-rad 'nan)))
                     (/ opp (geom/sin angle-rad)))
                    ((and (not (eq? adj 'nan)) (not (eq? angle-rad 'nan)))
                     (/ adj (geom/cos angle-rad)))
                    ((and (not (eq? opp 'nan)) (not (eq? adj 'nan)))
                     (sqrt (+ (* opp opp) (* adj adj))))
                    (else hyp)))
         (new-opp (cond
                    ((and (not (eq? new-hyp 'nan)) (not (eq? angle-rad 'nan)))
                     (* new-hyp (geom/sin angle-rad)))
                    ((and (not (eq? adj 'nan)) (not (eq? angle-rad 'nan)))
<|fim_middle|>                     (* adj (geom/tan angle-rad)))
                    (else opp)))
         (new-adj (cond
                    ((and (not (eq? new-hyp 'nan)) (not (eq? angle-rad 'nan)))
                     (* new-hyp (geom/cos angle-rad)))
                    ((and (not (eq? new-opp 'nan)) (not (eq? angle-rad 'nan)))
                     (/ new-opp (geom/tan angle-rad)))
                    (else adj)))
         (new-angle-rad (cond
                          ((not (eq? angle-rad 'nan)) angle-rad)
                          ((and (not (eq? new-opp 'nan)) (not (eq? new-adj 'nan)))
                           (atan (/ new-opp new-adj)))
                          ((and (not (eq? new-opp 'nan)) (not (eq? new-hyp 'nan)))

    (newline)

    (display new-hyp)
    (newline)
    (display \"Angle: \")
    (display new-angle-deg)
    (display \"°\")
    (newline)))

(define (relu-vec v)

(define (relu-mask u)
  (map (lambda (i) (if (> (vec/ref u i) 0) 1 0))
       (iota (vec/dim u))))

  (define h  (relu-vec u1))
<|fim_middle|>  (define y  (vec/make (map + (matvec W2 h) b2)))
  (list u1 h y))

;; Backward pass, given a loss-gradient dL/dy
(define (backward W1 b1 W2 b2 x dL-dy activations)
  (define u1 (car activations))
  (define h  (cadr activations))
  (define y  (caddr activations))

  ;; Second layer: y = W2 h + b2
  (define dL-db2 (map (lambda (i) (vec/ref dL-dy i)) (iota (vec/dim dL-dy))))
  (define dL-dh  (matvec (transpose W2)
                         (vec/make dL-db2)))
  (define dL-dW2 (outer-product dL-db2
                                (map (lambda (i) (vec/ref h i))
                                     (iota (vec/dim h)))))

  (define mask (relu-mask u1))
  (define dL-du1
    (map (lambda (i)
           (* (list-ref dL-dh i) (list-ref mask i)))
         (iota (length dL-dh))))

  (define dL-db1 dL-du1)
  (define dL-dW1 (outer-product dL-du1
                                (map (lambda (i) (vec/ref x i))
                                     (iota (vec/dim x)))))
  (define dL-dx  (matvec (transpose W1) (vec/make dL-du1)))

  (list dL-dW1 dL-db1 dL-dW2 dL-db2 dL-dx))

  (define h  (cadr fwd))

<|fim_prefix|>;; Given a vector, subtract mean, divide by stddev, then apply gamma and beta.
(define (layernorm v gamma beta)
  (define d (vec/dim v))
  (define components (map (lambda (i) (vec/ref v i)) (iota d)))
  (define mean (/ (reduce + 0 components) d))
  (define centered (map (lambda (x) (- x mean)) components))
  (define variance (/ (reduce + 0 (map (lambda (c) (* c c)) centered)) d))
<|fim_middle|>  (define stddev (math/sqrt (+ variance 0.00001)))   ;; 0.00001 for numerical safety
  (define normalized (map (lambda (c) (/ c stddev)) centered))
  (map (lambda (i)
         (+ (* (list-ref normalized i) (list-ref gamma i))
            (list-ref beta i)))
       (iota d)))

    (map (lambda (i)
           (+ (* (list-ref normed i) (list-ref gamma i))
              (list-ref beta i)))

;;   Given qs, ks, vs (all lists of D-vectors), scale = sqrt(d_k)

    (fold vec-add
          (vec-scale (car vs) 0)

               (iota (length vs)))))

<|fim_prefix|>;; Two keys of a horizontal motion.
;; Key 1: figure at x=100, y=200
;; Key 2: figure at x=500, y=200
;; Number of frames between the keys: 11 (giving 12 frames total: key1 + 11 in-betweens + key2)

;; A timing chart is a list of fractions between 0 and 1 representing
;; the progress at each frame. A linear chart is (0/11, 1/11, ... 11/11).
;; A cushioned chart uses non-linear spacing.

(define (linear-chart n)
  (map (lambda (i) (/ i n)) (range 0 (+ n 1))))

<|fim_middle|>;; An ease-in-out chart: use a sigmoid-like curve
;; s-curve maps 0-1 to 0-1 with slow start and slow end
(define (s-curve x)
  ;; smoothstep: 3x^2 - 2x^3
  (- (* 3 x x) (* 2 x x x)))

(define (ease-in-out-chart n)
  (map (lambda (i) (s-curve (/ i n))) (range 0 (+ n 1))))

;; A very slow-in chart: cube the progress
(define (slow-in-chart n)
  (map (lambda (i) (expt (/ i n) 3)) (range 0 (+ n 1))))
<|fim_suffix|>
;; Given a chart, produce the position at each frame
(define (positions-from-chart chart x1 x2)
  (map (lambda (t) (+ x1 (* t (- x2 x1)))) chart))

;; Compare three motions of the same start and end points:
;; linear, ease-in-out, slow-in.
(define linear-motion    (positions-from-chart (linear-chart 11) 100 500))
(define eased-motion     (positions-from-chart (ease-in-out-chart 11) 100 500))
(define slow-in-motion   (positions-from-chart (slow-in-chart 11) 100 500))

;; linear-motion:    (100 136 173 209 245 281 318 354 390 427 463 500)
;; eased-motion:     (100 100 111 141 189 245 302 355 400 431 452 500)
;; slow-in-motion:   (100 100 100 101 106 118 141 178 235 313 415 500)

                     ((sad) 2)

;; Total duration: 96 frames at 24 fps = 4 seconds.
;; Beginning (frames 0-24): character walks in from the left.

    ;; Beginning: character walks in from left

     (world/place-character 146 300 'looking-right)
     (world/place-object 200 300 'highlighted))

    ;; Middle: emotional reaction — character reads as delighted
    ((< frame 72)
     (let ((bob (* 8 (sin (* (- frame 48) 0.5)))))
       (world/place-character 146 (- 300 bob) 'delighted)
       (world/place-object 200 300 'highlighted)))

<|fim_suffix|>    (else
     (let ((x (+ 146 (* (- frame 72) 6))))
       (world/place-character x 300 'walking))

         (first-duration (* total-duration first-fraction))
         (second-duration (* total-duration second-fraction)))

    (note-play-for note2 second-duration)))

## 11.10 Reaching for What You Don't Know — Anchoring Percussion in a Movement

Every drum tradition arrived somewhere. A clave belongs to Cuban son; a taiko roll belongs to Japanese festival drumming; a tabla teental belongs to Hindustani classical. When you author a groove, you can reach for the movement atom that names the tradition — a small side-step that keeps the code honest about where the rhythm came from.

### Citing the tradition beside the pattern

You lay down a clave pattern. In the same expression, reach for the movement — so the operator (and your future self) knows the pattern isn't invented, it's inherited.

        (velocity-piano 0.65))

    ;; Grace note into a trill on E5
    (note/strike 'D5 0.05 velocity-forte)
    (trill-cadenza 'E5 'F5 1.0 12 velocity-forte)
    
    ;; Descending arpeggio (C E G C, reversed)
    (arpeggio-cadenza '(C5 G4 E4 C4) 0.15 velocity-piano)

    (tremolo-cadenza 'G3 1.5 16 velocity-forte)

    (glissando-stepped-cadenza 'C3 'C5 32 velocity-forte)

    (note/strike 'C4 3.0 velocity-forte)
    (note/strike 'C5 3.0 velocity-forte)))

                  (trill-loop (+ n 1) other-pitch current-pitch)))))
      (trill-loop 0 pitch1 pitch2))))

  (let ((note-dur (/ tremolo-dur subdivisions)))
    (letrec ((tremolo-loop 
              (lambda (n)
                (when (< n subdivisions)
                  (note/strike pitch note-dur velocity)
                  (tremolo-loop (+ n 1))))))
      (tremolo-loop 0))))

(define (analyze-contour pitches)

      ((equal? p 'E4) 64)
<|fim_middle|>      ((equal? p 'F4) 65)

<|fim_suffix|>    (if (< (length ps) 2)
        '()
        (cons (- (pitch->midi (cadr ps))
                 (pitch->midi (car ps)))
              (intervals (cdr ps)))))
  (intervals pitches))

      ((= m 76) 'E5)
      ((= m 77) 'F5)
      ((= m 79) 'G5)
      (else 'C4)))
  (define (pitch->midi p)
    (cond
      ((equal? p 'C4) 60)

      ((equal? p 'F4) 65)
